documents.title: SQL ANY Operator
documents.summary: Compare a value against a subquery list so the condition passes if true for AT LEAST ONE returned value.
documents.definition_text: ANY / SOME Operator: Subquery comparison returning TRUE if the comparison holds for at least one value returned by the subquery. `value > ANY (SELECT ...)` evaluates to TRUE if `value` is greater than at least one item in the subquery (equivalent to being greater than the minimum value). Note: In SQLite (used in our practice engine), `> ANY (subquery)` is written equivalently as `> (SELECT MIN(...) FROM ...)` or `EXISTS`.
documents.example_text: Finding products cheaper than ANY flagship model in PostgreSQL/MySQL. Example: SELECT full_name, salary FROM instructors WHERE salary > (SELECT MIN(salary) FROM instructors WHERE dept_id = 'CS');

documents.practical_explanation: SQLite equivalent of `salary > ANY (SELECT salary ...)`: beats the lowest CS salary.

documents.title: SQL ALL Operator
documents.summary: Require a value comparison to hold against EVERY single item returned by a subquery using ALL.
documents.definition_text: ALL Operator: Subquery comparison returning TRUE only if the comparison holds for every single row returned. `value > ALL (SELECT ...)` is TRUE only if `value` exceeds EVERY value returned by the subquery (equivalent to `> MAX(...)`). In SQLite, express `> ALL (SELECT col ...)` using `> (SELECT MAX(col) ...)` or `NOT EXISTS`.
documents.example_text: Finding instructors earning more than ALL Electrical Engineering instructors. Example: SELECT full_name, salary FROM instructors WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructors WHERE dept_id = 'EC');
documents.diagram_config_json: {"layers":[{"id":"u3_1","label":"1. Execution Outcome","role":"Finds instructors paid strictly more than every EC instructor.","sample":"`> ALL` means greater than every value (equivalent to `> MAX`); beware of NULLs in the subquery."}]}
documents.practical_sql: SELECT full_name, salary FROM instructors WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructors WHERE dept_id = 'EC');
documents.practical_explanation: Finds instructors paid strictly more than every EC instructor.
documents.lesson_content_json: {"simpleIntro":"While ANY asks if you beat at least one value, ALL asks if you beat EVERY single value in the list.","detailedExplanation":"`value > ALL (SELECT ...)` is TRUE only if `value` exceeds EVERY value returned by the subquery (equivalent to `> MAX(...)`). In SQLite, express `> ALL (SELECT col ...)` using `> (SELECT MAX(col) ...)` or `NOT EXISTS`.","definitions":[{"term":"ALL Operator","meaning":"Subquery comparison returning TRUE only if the comparison holds for every single row returned."}],"realWorldExamples":["Finding instructors earning more than ALL Electrical Engineering instructors."],"practicalExamples":[{"label":"SQL ALL Operator","snippet":"SELECT full_name, salary FROM instructors WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructors WHERE dept_id = 'EC');","outcome":"Finds instructors paid strictly more than every EC instructor.\n\nExpected SQLite output on the seeded practice database: columns [\"full_name\",\"salary\"]; first rows [[\"Dr. Ada Lovelace\",135000],[\"Dr. Edgar Codd\",142000],[\"Dr. Grace Hopper\",138000]]; 3 row(s) total."}],"visualSteps":[{"step":"01","title":"Goal","detail":"Require a value comparison to hold against EVERY single item returned by a subquery using ALL."},{"step":"02","title":"SQL Pattern","detail":"SELECT full_name, salary FROM instructors WHERE salary > (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM instructors WHERE dept_id = 'EC');"},{"step":"03","title":"Result","detail":"Finds instructors paid strictly more than every EC instructor."}],"commonMistakes":["Forgetting that if a subquery for `ALL` returns a NULL, `value > ALL` evaluates to UNKNOWN (false)!"],"quickRecap":["`> ALL` means greater than every value (equivalent to `> MAX`); beware of NULLs in the subquery."],"advantages":["The ALL operator lets you state a “greater‑than‑every” condition in a single predicate, eliminating the need for multiple ORed comparisons. This shortens the query and makes the intent immediately clear to readers.","Database optimizers can rewrite ALL into an aggregate such as MAX or into a NOT EXISTS test, which often runs faster than scanning each row individually. Consequently, CPU cycles and I/O are saved on large subqueries.","ALL works consistently with numeric, date, and character columns, so the same logical pattern can be reused across diverse data types. This uniformity reduces the learning curve and keeps application code tidy."],"disadvantages":["SQLite does not implement ALL directly, forcing you to rewrite the predicate using MAX or NOT EXISTS, which adds cognitive overhead and extra lines of code. Porting such queries to other RDBMS can therefore introduce bugs.","When the subquery returns NULL values, ALL evaluates to UNKNOWN, causing rows to be filtered out even though the numeric comparison appears valid. Developers must explicitly handle NULLs, complicating the query logic.","Some engines materialize the entire subquery before applying the ALL comparison, which can consume significant memory for very large result sets. In those cases, performance may degrade compared to a correlated EXISTS approach."]}

documents.title: SQL EXISTS
documents.summary: Test efficiently whether a correlated subquery returns at least one matching row using EXISTS.
documents.definition_text: EXISTS Operator: Boolean predicate returning TRUE if a subquery yields at least one row. `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ... WHERE ...)` returns TRUE if the subquery produces one or more rows, and FALSE if it returns zero rows. Because it short-circuits on the first match, EXISTS is often faster than IN on large tables.
documents.example_text: Listing customers who have placed at least one order in 2026. Example: SELECT d.dept_name FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects p WHERE p.dept_id = d.dept_id);

Execution Outcome","role":"Returns departments that sponsor at least one research project.","sample":"EXISTS returns TRUE as soon as its correlated subquery finds 1 matching row."}]}
documents.practical_sql: SELECT d.dept_name FROM departments d WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM projects p WHERE p.dept_id = d.dept_id);
documents.practical_explanation: Returns departments that sponsor at least one research project.
